Interface LocatedHttpBodyRouteSpec<T, B extends @Nullable Object>

Type Parameters:
T - The type of the located target
B - The type of the body the handler receives
All Superinterfaces:
ExecutionSpec<HttpBodyRouteSpec<B>>, HttpBodyRouteSpec<B>, RouteFilterSpec<HttpBodyRouteSpec<B>>, RouteSpec<HttpBodyRouteSpec<B>>
public sealed interface LocatedHttpBodyRouteSpec<T, B extends @Nullable Object> extends HttpBodyRouteSpec<B>
The pending route of the routes of a located target after a body stage, see LocatedHttpRouteSpec: an HttpBodyRouteSpec whose settings return the located route, and whose terminals also take a handler that receives the located target and the body.
Since:
5.3.0
Author:
Denis Stepanov

  • Method Details

    • consumes

      LocatedHttpBodyRouteSpec<T,B> consumes(MediaType... mediaTypes)
      Description copied from interface: RouteSpec
      Accept requests with these media types only, like @Consumes on a controller method, or on a controller for a group.

      On a group, the routes of the group, and of its nested groups, consume them instead of application/json. A route that declares what it consumes, with this method or RouteSpec.consumesAll(), and a nested group that does, replace them, like a method-level @Consumes replaces the one of its controller. So does a form route, e.g. HttpRouteSpec.form(), which consumes the form media types: a form handler reads a form.

      routes.path("/notes", notes -> {
    notes.consumes(MediaType.TEXT_PLAIN_TYPE).produces(MediaType.TEXT_PLAIN_TYPE);
    notes.POST("/").body(String.class).handle((request, pathVariables, text) -> HttpResponse.ok(notes.save(text)));
    notes.POST("/json")
        .consumes(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON_TYPE)
        .body(Note.class).handle((request, pathVariables, note) -> HttpResponse.ok(notes.save(note)));
});

      The media types, and the executor, see ExecutionSpec.executeOn(String), of a group apply to its routes to handlers, including the implicit HEAD routes, the routes declared for several methods and the declared routes, and to the routes its locator routes locate, unless they, or a group of their LocatedRoutes, declare their own; not to its error and status routes.

      Specified by:
      consumes in interface RouteSpec<T>
      Parameters:
      mediaTypes - The media types
      Returns:
      The route or the group

    • annotationMetadata

      LocatedHttpBodyRouteSpec<T,B> annotationMetadata(AnnotationMetadataProvider annotationMetadata)
      Description copied from interface: RouteSpec
      Give the route the annotations of an annotated element: the features that read the annotations of the matched route, such as security rules, versioning, filter binding, route conditions and the message body writers, see them as if they were on a controller method, and so does the return type of the route.

      When the element is an ExecutableMethod, e.g. a method of a resource that a framework integration routes with handler functions, the route implements that bean method: besides its annotations, the target method, declaring type and method name of the route are the ones of the bean method, so the local @Error methods of the bean class apply to the route, and the route is described as the bean method. The arguments of the route stay those of the handler. Any other element, e.g. a BeanDefinition, gives the route its annotations only.

      ExecutableMethod<Payments, String> pay = beanContext.getBeanDefinition(Payments.class).getRequiredMethod("pay", long.class);
routes.POST("/payments/{amount}")
    .annotationMetadata(pay)
    .handle((request, pathVariables) -> HttpResponse.ok(payments.pay(pathVariables.getLong("amount"))));

      The route keeps the element: an integration finds it back on the matched route with MethodBasedRouteInfo.getAnnotationMetadataProvider(), and the bean method of the route with instanceof ExecutableMethod. The last element given to the route wins.

      On a group, the element is the default element of the routes of the group, and of its nested groups, to handlers: a route without its own element has the one of its innermost group that has one, as if it were given to the route, e.g. the BeanDefinition of a resource for every route of the resource. The element of a route, or of a nested group, replaces it. The annotations given with RouteSpec.annotate(AnnotationValue) to the groups and to the route override the ones of the element.

      Specified by:
      annotationMetadata in interface RouteSpec<T>
      Parameters:
      annotationMetadata - The annotated element whose annotations the route has, an ExecutableMethod for a route that implements a bean method
      Returns:
      The route or the group

    • annotate

      <A extends Annotation> LocatedHttpBodyRouteSpec<T,B> annotate(AnnotationValue<A> annotationValue)
      Description copied from interface: RouteSpec
      Annotate the route with an annotation, like an annotation on a controller method, with the annotate methods of the compile-time elements, e.g. io.micronaut.inject.ast.Element#annotate: the features that read the annotations of the matched route see it, e.g. a @FilterMatcher annotation binds its filters to the route, and @Version selects the route by the version of the request. Several annotations are chained calls. 
      routes.POST("/payments/{amount}")
    .annotate(Audited.class)
    .annotate(Version.class, version -> version.value("2"))
    .handle(payHandler);

      If the route already has the annotation, the members of the given one are merged with, and override, the existing ones; a repeatable annotation is added to the existing ones. The annotations of the route are layered like the annotations of a controller method over the ones of its class: the annotations of the element given with RouteSpec.annotationMetadata(AnnotationMetadataProvider), then of the groups of the route, outer group first, then of the route, each overriding the members of the same annotation before it.

      On a group, the routes of the group, and of its nested groups, have the annotation; the annotation of a nested group or of a route overrides the members it sets.

      The meta-annotations of an annotation type are not known at runtime: a feature that looks up an annotation by its own type sees it, like the ones above, @CrossOrigin, @ExecuteOn or a security annotation, but a feature that looks up a stereotype of the annotation needs the stereotype in the annotation value, see AnnotationValueBuilder.stereotype(AnnotationValue). The expressions of an annotation, e.g. of @RouteCondition, are compiled with the annotated code: a route condition is declared with RouteSpec.where(RouteCondition).

      Specified by:

      LocatedHttpBodyRouteSpec<T,B> attribute(String name, Object value)
      Description copied from interface: RouteSpec
      Give the route an attribute: metadata of the route for the code that handles its requests, which reads it from the matched route with RouteInfo.getAttribute(String), e.g. a route filter, a server filter or the handler. They are the attributes of the route, not of the request, see RouteAttributes for the route of a request.

      On a group, the routes of the group, and of its nested groups, have the attribute, and so do the routes its locator routes locate; the attribute of a nested group, of a route, or of a located route or a group of its LocatedRoutes, with the same name overrides it.

      routes.path("/admin", admin -> {
    admin.attribute("role", "admin");
    admin.GET("/users", usersHandler);
    admin.GET("/audit").attribute("role", "auditor").handle(auditHandler);
});
routes.serverFilter("/admin/**").beforeReplacing(request -> {
    String role = RouteAttributes.getRouteInfo(request)
        .flatMap(route -> route.getAttribute("role", String.class))
        .orElseThrow();
    return hasRole(request, role) ? null : HttpResponse.status(HttpStatus.FORBIDDEN);
});

    • where

      LocatedHttpBodyRouteSpec<T,B> where(RouteCondition condition)
      Description copied from interface: RouteSpec
      Match the requests that meet a condition only, like @RouteCondition on a controller method: a request the condition rejects is answered as if the route did not exist, by another route of the same URI and method, e.g. one with another condition, or by 404, never by a 405, 415 or 406 of this route. The conditions are evaluated while the request is matched, for every request whose path the route matches: they must be fast and must not block, nor read the body. 
      routes.GET("/reports/{id}")
    .where(RouteCondition.header("X-Export", "csv"))
    .handle((request, pathVariables) -> HttpResponse.ok(reports.csv(pathVariables.getLong("id"))));
routes.GET("/reports/{id}", (request, pathVariables) -> HttpResponse.ok(reports.find(pathVariables.getLong("id"))));

      A request both routes of the example match, with the header, is ambiguous: the most specific route answers it, and the two routes are equally specific, so it is answered with 400. RouteCondition builds conditions on the headers, query parameters, cookies, method, host, client address and time of the request, and RequestPredicates on its media types too.

      On a group, the condition applies to the routes of the group, including its locator routes and the routes of its nested groups: a route matches a request that meets the conditions of its groups and its own, which must all be met, as one all condition. Several conditions of a route or a group must all be met too. The router evaluates them cheapest first, the custom conditions last, in the order they were declared, outer group first.

      Specified by:
      where in interface RouteSpec<T>
      Parameters:
      condition - The condition
      Returns:
      The route or the group

    • constrain

      LocatedHttpBodyRouteSpec<T,B> constrain(Predicate<? super PathVariables> accepted)
      Description copied from interface: RouteSpec
      Constrain the path variables of the route: the route matches a request only when the constraint accepts the path variables its URI template bound. Otherwise the route is not a match, as if its URI template did not match: the request goes on to the other routes, e.g. a route with the same URI template, or is answered with 404 when none matches. 
      routes.path("/shops/{shop}", shop -> shop
    .constrain("shop", SHOPS)
    .GET("/stock", stockHandler));
routes.GET("/orders/{id}")
    .constrain("id", Long.class, id -> id > 0)
    .handle(ordersHandler);

      A constraint runs while the request is matched, after the URI template of the route matched and bound the variables, before the media types, the conditions, see RouteSpec.where(RouteCondition), and the ambiguity between the routes are considered. It is given the same PathVariables the handler is given. Since a rejected route is not a match, the methods allowed on a path for a 405, the media types for a 415 or 406, a CORS preflight request and the implicit HEAD route consider only the routes whose constraints pass: a rejected value never produces a 405. A constraint that throws an exception, e.g. a variable that does not convert, rejects the variables; the exception is logged at debug level.

      A constraint should be cheap, and must not have side effects: it runs for every request the URI template of the route matches, including the requests another route answers. A route without constraints costs nothing more to match.

      On a group, the constraint applies to the routes of the group, including the routes of its nested groups: the constraints of the groups, outer group first, and of the route must all pass.

      Specified by:
      constrain in interface RouteSpec<T>
      Parameters:
      accepted - Whether the path variables are accepted
      Returns:
      The route or the group

    • order

      LocatedHttpBodyRouteSpec<T,B> order(int order)
      Description copied from interface: RouteSpec
      Break a tie with other routes that are equally good for a request: the route with the lowest order answers it. The router keeps the routes that explicitly produce the media type the request accepts first, then, for a request with a body, the routes that explicitly consume its content type, then the routes with the most specific URI template; it then prefers a route of the request's method over a route of any method, and an explicit HEAD route over an implicit one; only the routes still left after that are compared by their order. So the order never makes a less specific route, or a route of any method over a route of the request's method, win: it chooses among routes of the same URI template whose conditions a request both meets, e.g. a specialized route and a fallback. Two routes left with the same order still make the request ambiguous, answered with 400. 
      routes.GET("/reports/{id}")
    .where(RequestPredicates.queryParam("format", "csv"))
    .order(-1)
    .handle(csvHandler);
routes.GET("/reports/{id}", reportHandler); // the order 0: answers the other requests

      The order is global: it is compared between any routes left for a request, controller routes and the routes of every HttpRoutes bean and group alike, and the lower order wins. The default order is 0, the order of a controller route, so a route with a negative order wins a tie with a controller route and one with a positive order loses it. On a group, the order is the default of the routes of the group, and of its nested groups, unless they or a nested group have their own. The order of an HttpRoutes bean orders the beans, not their routes.

      Specified by:
      order in interface RouteSpec<T>
      Parameters:
      order - The order, lower wins
      Returns:
      The route or the group

    • port

      LocatedHttpBodyRouteSpec<T,B> port(int port)
      Description copied from interface: RouteSpec
      Route the requests on this port only, like @Controller(port = ...): the server opens the port when it starts, and the route does not match a request on another port, which is answered as if the route did not exist. A route without a port matches the requests on the default ports of the server only, once a route of the application has a port. 
      routes.GET("/metrics")
    .port(9090)
    .handle((request, pathVariables) -> HttpResponse.ok(metrics.scrape()));

      On a group, the routes of the group, including its locator routes and the routes of its nested groups, inherit the port; a nested group or a route with its own port overrides it. Located routes cannot open a port: their routes cannot have one.

      port - The port, between 1 and 65535: unlike @Controller(port = ...), a negative port or 0, a random port the route could not match, is rejected

    • executeOn

      LocatedHttpBodyRouteSpec<T,B> executeOn(String executorName)
      Description copied from interface: ExecutionSpec
      Run the code on the named executor, like @ExecuteOn. It applies whatever the thread selection of the server.

      On a route, the handler runs on the executor, like @ExecuteOn on a controller method. On a group, the routes of the group, and of its nested groups, run on it, like @ExecuteOn on a controller, unless they, or a nested group, choose their thread. The media types and the executor of a group apply to its routes to handlers, including the implicit HEAD routes, the routes declared for several methods and the declared routes, and to the routes its locator routes locate, unless they, or a group of their LocatedRoutes, choose their own; not to its error and status routes.

      On a filter, the filter runs on the executor, like a filter method annotated @ExecuteOn: use it for a filter that blocks, e.g. on a database. The filter chain continues on that executor. An asynchronous filter is called on the executor, and the filter chain continues where its stage completes.

      Specified by:
      executeOn in interface ExecutionSpec<T>
      Parameters:
      executorName - The name of the executor, e.g. TaskExecutors.BLOCKING
      Returns:
      The route, the group or the filter

    • nonBlocking

      LocatedHttpBodyRouteSpec<T,B> nonBlocking()
      Description copied from interface: ExecutionSpec
      Run the code without switching the thread. On a route, the handler runs on the event loop, like @NonBlocking on a controller method, when the server selects threads automatically: the route must not block.     • before

      LocatedBodyFilterSpec<T,B> before(RouteRequestFilter filter)
      Description copied from interface: RouteFilterSpec
      Filter the requests, like a @RequestFilter method that returns nothing. The filters of a route and of its groups run after the server filters, closest to the route: the filters of the outer group first, then those of the inner groups, then those of the route, each in the order they are declared. The filter of a route or a group runs only when the route, or a route of the group, matched the request: not for a 404 or a 405 under the prefix of the group, which only the server filters, pre-matching ones included, see.
      Specified by:
      before in interface RouteFilterSpec<T>
      Parameters:
      filter - The filter, which can change the request in place
      Returns:
      The filter, to choose where it runs and to go back to the route or the group, see FilterSpec
      See Also:
      • RouteRequestFilter
